segments.text: Structural and chromatographic characterization of cation‑exchange membranes based on carboxymethyl/ nanofibrillated cellulose using lysozyme
Vanja Kokol · Tina Simčič · Urh Černigoj
Received: 8 September 2024 / Accepted: 14 February 2025 / Published online: 4 March 2025 © The Author(s) 2025

Abstract Bio-based membranes are becoming highly-desired low-cost, environmentally friendly, and readily available supports for the separation and purification of biomacromolecules. In this work, weak cation-exchange and highly (> 95%) microporous (> 80 μm) cellulose-based membranes were prepared from different weight ratios of carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) as anionic polymer and cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) as a stabilizing and structural filler, by the freeze-casting process and citric-acid (CA) mediated in situ cross-linking (esterification). It was ascertained that mono-esterified/grafted CA also contributes to the total carboxylic groups (1.7–2.6 mmol/g), while the CMC-induced CNF orientation affected the membrane’s morphology and lysozyme (Lys) binding capacity. A static binding capacity (SBC) between 370 and 1080 mg/g, and equilibrium within 3.3 h for 1 g/mL Lys was thus achieved with increasing the total solid and CMC content by forming more

isotropic microporous structures. The selected membranes were then packed in a chromatographic housing, analyzed for pressure drop, and evaluated for dynamic binding capacity (DBC), depending on the process performance (flow rates, Lys concentration). A DBC in the 165–417 mg/g range was determined at a throughput of 0.5 mL/min, and elution yield of 78–99% with > 95% recovery. The Lys adsorption and transfer were reduced by the increasing flow rate and membrane density due to compressibility issues, resulting in smaller and irregularly distributed pores and the unavailability of carboxylic groups. Although the DBC was still comparable with the commercial CIM® monoliths, the convection-based transport of molecules inside the membrane and the membrane stiffness needs to be improved in further research.

Keywords Cation-exchange membrane · Cellulose nanofibrils · Carboxymethyl cellulose · Citric acid · Lysozyme · Static and dynamic binding capacity

The chromatographic purification of biopharmaceuticals is still driven by higher productivity, lower production costs, and increased speed for the development and validation of the purification cycles, which are required by using existing non-biodegradable packed beds of microporous polymeric resins or polymeric chromatographic monoliths. The increased use of low-cost, ready-to-use adsorption membranes or filters, which may act as a complementary method to the existing systems in current downstream processes with high enough performance and economic feasibility, is thus becoming of high interest. The membranes and monoliths, namely, opposite to traditional resin systems, operate at higher flow rates with faster adsorption kinetics due to the greatly reduced bed heights and because the adsorption takes place mainly on the membrane surface (Chen et al. 2020).

In the last decade, many efforts have thus been dedicated to the construction of ease-packed and highly 3D porous fibrous scaffolds/mats prepared from polymeric solutions by electrospinning, followed by their stabilization and surface-modification with ion-exchange ligands (Saxena et. al. 2009; Wang et al. 2013; Chang et al. 2021). Electro-spun nanofiber membranes with high enough porosity, larger surface area, robust mechanical strength, and versatility in terms of surface functionalization have been suggested to increase the protein adsorption selectivity, immobilization efficiency, ion exchange, and hydrophobicity at reduced pressure drops, thus enhancing their long-term stability and reusability (Fu et al. 2018). For instance, Cibacron blue F3GA functionalized poly(ether sulfone) membranes (Ma et al. 2009) have been studied, along with concentrated nitric acid and surfactant-treated carbon nanofibers (Schneiderman et al. 2011), poly(isobutylene-b-styrene) membranes (Casiano-Maldonado et al. 2013), multi-layered electro-spun regenerated cellulose (Dods et al. 2015), citric acid modified electro-spun ethylene–vinyl alcohol (Fu et al. 2016), and maleic anhydride electro-spun grafted cellulose (Ma et al. 2015). The relatively high static (160–284 mg/g) and dynamic (118–250 mg/g) adsorption capacity

of lysozyme (Lys)—generally used as a model protein—with good reversibility and low-pressure drops (< kPa) was thus achieved (Ma et. al. 2015; Fu et al. 2016), which matched well with the requirements for protein purification, although requiring a long time (6–12 h) to reach equilibrium. However, electrospinning involves complex processes that apply high-voltage electric fields with low production rates (Khan and Hassan 2021), thus facing scalability and cost-effectiveness challenges, making them difficult to commercialize at scale.

The use of sustainable and environmentally friendly materials, with the potential for their reuse and recycling after end-of-life, are becoming additional requirements under the new eco-design regulation (ESPR, 2024/1781) directive to foster product circularity. However, although cellulose and its modified analogs are already widely used chromatographic supports because of their biocompatibility, stability, and easy modification with varied ion-exchanged ligands (Kadokawa et al. 2008, Du et al. 2010), they are still prepared by non-green ionic liquids—based double emulsification via phase separation (Du et al. 2010). Hence, the density of functional groups on these membranes is not adjustable, rendering a restriction in their operating flexibility and processing time (i.e. the relatively low adsorption capacity at too-long adsorption kinetics, Khan et al. 2024), high operation pressure-drops, and the usage of large quantities of solvents due to the slow intra-structure microsphere diffusion. Low-cost and readily available microporous cellulose-based membranes in macromolecule purification thus represent a superior alternative to traditional polymeric ones, but they are still in the development phase. The low manufacturing costs of membranes would also make them compatible with a single-use approach.

Freeze-casting (also known as ice templating) has emerged as one of the most cost-effective and environmentally friendly technologies (Stratta et al. 2020), which is expected to grow additionally by 8.6% by 2034 according to the market forecast. Freeze-casting was already established as a powerful consolidation technique for the fabrication of sophisticated (macro)porous and layered hybrid materials, including porous scaffolds and high-performance membranes (Scotti and Dunand 2018). However, the transition towards their commercialization still requires improvements in reproducibility and, due to
expensive initial investment, the ability to up-scale economically, especially optimizing the use cycles over the lifetime of the device, rather than simply reducing energy consumption.

In our previous research, highly porous (> 95%), water- and compression-stable cation-exchange membranes were introduced, fabricated by a freeze-casting process using cellulose nanofibrils (CNF) and citric acid (CA) acting as a crosslinker (in situ esterification) and source of weak anionic (carboxylic, –COOH) surface groups arising from the mono-esterified CA (Kokol and Vivod 2023). The membrane’s morphological structure with accessible surface-positioned functional groups was shown to be significant for the proteins’ specific (related to the net charged and molecular weight) adsorption dynamic (> 52% of positive Lysozyme Cytochrome, < 8% of negative BSA/Myoglobin) at extremely high flux rates (> 3.000 hL/h*MPa*m2), as well as their regeneration (desorption, > 97%) and membrane re-equilibration (NaCl) with flux recovery (> 80%) after 5 consecutive filtration cycles by using dead-end filtration mode performed with a 0.05 MPa head pressure.

Considering such a performance of the as-prepared CNF-based membranes, in this work, their efficacy as cation-exchanges for positively charged Lys was studied after introducing the carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) to increase the binding sites, following the criteria that would enable their chromatographic application similar to monoliths (Podgornik et al. 2013). In addition, the variation of their (CNF and CMC) weight ratio, together with the total weight of the solid and CA addition, was modulated to reveal the membrane’s charge and porosity, affecting the Lys binding capacity and transport. The membranes were analyzed further for static (equilibrium) Lys binding capacities (SBC), as well as dynamic binding capacities (DBC) at different flow rates under the chromatographic conditions, thus to gain an understanding of the overall performance of these types of cationexchange membrane absorbers.
Cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) with chain-like structures within diameters of the 10–70 nm range and

lengths of a few (1–3 μm) micrometers were prepared as water-dispersed hydrogel by the refining of bleached softwood pulp in a multistage disc refiner at the University of Maine (USA), The Process Development Center. Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) of high viscosity (700–1500 mPas at 1%wt) and substitution degree of 0.6–0.95, anhydrous citric acid (CA), lysozyme (Lys; Mw of 14.31 kDa as provided by the manufacturer, the isoelectric point at pH 11.35 as determined by potentiometric titration described below, and zeta potential of 4.7 ± 0.5 mV in 20 mM Tris-buffer at pH 8 as determined by Dynamic Light Scattering analysis using Zetasizer, Nano ZS ZEN360, Malvern Instruments Ltd., UK, respectively), Tris–HCl and NaCl, were purchased from Sigma Aldrich Co. Ltd. (USA), and used without further purification.
The membrane preparation process is presented in Fig. 1, according to our previous study (Gorgieva et al. 2019). The CMC was dissolved in deionized

water at 2 wt% concentration at room temperature (23 ± 1 °C) by 24 h of magnetic stirring, until achieving a moderately viscous and transparent solution. In parallel, the CNF suspension was water dispersed to a 2 wt% concentration for 3 min at 7000 min−1 by using a homogenizer, Ultra-Turrax T18 (IKA-Werke GmbH & Co.KG, Germany). The mixtures from different volume ratios of CNF dispersion (2–12 mL) and CMC solution (1–12 mL) were prepared, following the addition of a (1.2–3.6 mL) CA solution of 5–50 wt/wt% concentration in respect to the total weight masses of both CNFs and CMC, and the addition of the required mL of milli-Q water to the final 30.6 mL, by homogenization for up to 1 min using a Vortex (IKA MS 3 Basic, IKA-Werke GmbH & Co. KG, Germany) at 2.500 rpm, before being poured into a polystyrene Petri dish (Greiner Bio-one GmbH, Austria) of 90 cm in diameter. The samples were subjected to freezing for 24 h in a freezer at about − 20 °C, followed by lyophilization (Mini Lyotrap, LTE Scientific Ltd, UK) to process them into porous membranes, and then dried further (Univerzal oven UM 400, Memmert GmbH, Germany) for 24 h at

The obtained membranes were immersed in excess amounts of milli-Q water overnight, followed by rinsing at least three times to remove the unreacted CA molecules. This was followed by pH and conductivity measurements (HANNA HI 8733, Hanna instruments SI, Slovenia), and UV–Vis measurement (230–400 nm) using a microplate reader, Infinite M200 (Tecan GmbH, Austria). The membranes were refrigeratorstored (in wet conditions) before further usage unless otherwise specified. The membranes were designated according to the total solid weight, as well as to the weight percentage of CMC and CNFs, recalculated related to the total volume, e.g., the membrane M5, designed as CMC:CNF = 5.9:5.9 (total 1.18 wt%). This means that the sample was prepared with 9 mL of 2 wt% CMC (total 0.59 wt%), 9 mL of 2 wt% CNFs (total 0.59 wt%), 3.6 mL of 10 wt/wt% CA and 9 mL of milli-Q water (total 30.6 mL). An overview of the experimental design for the preparation of membranes is collected in Table 1.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging

The high-resolution images of differently prepared membranes (freeze-dried after 1 h of wetting in milli- Q, unless otherwise specified) were performed using a Sirion 400NC (FEI, USA) microscope. The pore diameter was evaluated from the obtained micrographs by using the Image J. Pro6.2 software program, and a minimum of 25 pores were selected for each evaluation. The final pore diameter size for each
sample was taken as the arithmetic mean and Standard Deviation.

Potentiometric titration of milli-Q water-suspended CNFs, CMC and CA, and differently prepared membranes was performed, to quantify the processingdependent esterification degree and surface charge contribution. The titration was carried out using a dual-burette instrument, (Mettler Toledo T-70), equipped with a combined glass electrode, (Mettler TDG 117, Metter Toledo d.o.o., Slovenia), within an inert (N2) atmosphere. The burettes were filled with 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M KOH (Merck d.o.o., Slovenia). The titration was carried out at room temperature (23 ± 1 °C) in forward and back runs between pH 2 and 11. Different titrant volumes (0.001–0.25 mL) were added dynamically within 30–80 s periods. Blank HCl–KOH titration was carried out under the same conditions. The molar concentration relating to the overall charge of the weak ions was calculated from the potentiometric titration data. All the reported values are the mean values of duplicate determinations.

Mercury-intrusion porosimetry was applied to determine the total porosity (%), pore size distribution, average pore diameter (µm), total specific surface area (SSA, m2/g), bulk and skeletal density (g/cm3) of the selected membranes (approximate dimensions 1 × 1 cm), by using the Pascal 140 computeraided Mercury Intrusion Porosimeter (Thermo Fisher

The wet compression strength tests of the selected membranes (1 × 1 cm) were performed by using a ZwickRoel electro-dynamic testing machine LTM3 (Zwick GmbH & Co., Germany) at a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min. The membranes were analyzed as 1 h pre-hydrated in the MPA solution.
Membrane performance testing
Static lysozyme binding capacity (SBC)—adsorption under static conditions

Defined pieces (1 × 1 cm) of the membranes were equilibrated in MPA (20 mM TRIS of pH 8.0), and then placed in a 10 mL glass tube containing 1, 5 or 10 mg/mL of Lys dispersed in MPA. The tubes were placed on a shaker bath (50 rpm, 21 ± 1 °C) for 24/48 h, which was determined by the experiment to be enough time to reach equilibrium. A calibration curve between the UV absorbance (at 280 nm) and concentration was used, to measure the final concentration of Lys adsorption efficacy (Ads), the adsorption binding capacity (BC), and adsorption quantity (Q), according to Eqs. 1, 2 and 3, respectively:
where C0 and Ct(mg/mL) are the concentrations of Lys for the initial and after pre-determined incubation times (t), V is the volume of Lys solution (mL), and m is the dry mass of the membrane (g).
Flow permeability experiments using a chromatography module

The pressure drop along the membrane packed in a 1200 Infinity LC system (Agilent Techn. Inc, USA) was recorded at different flow velocities (Φ, between 0.5–3.0 mL/min) using mobile phase A (MPA: 20 mM TRIS of pH 8.0). The membrane (circle, 16 mm in diameter) was loaded into a dedicated plastic housing, enabling good distribution of the mobile phase onto the membrane inlet surface, and placed as a column in the HPLC system. The pressure drop on the column was followed with a differential manometer (Valydine, Northridge, USA) throughout the whole chromatographic run. The relationship of the pressure-flow rate was evaluated.
Chromatographic tests with lysozyme

Bind‑elute (BE) testing The membranes were packed into a dedicated plastic column housing and inserted in the HPLC system as described above. The signal was monitored by UV detector at 280 nm. Membranes were washed with 5 mL MPB (20 mM Tris-buffer and 2 M NaCl of pH 8.0), followed by 5 mL MPA. Then 20 µL of Lys solution at different concentrations (0.5–2 mg/mL Lys in MPA) was injected at 0.5 mL/ min.. The unbound Lys was determined by washing the membrane using MPA, followed by a step change to MPB to elute the bound Lys. The evaluation of protein binding (leakage, bind-elute / BE test) and mass balance were calculated from the areas of unbound and eluted peaks according to Eqs. (4) and (5). The column was regenerated between each run by treating it for 10 min with MPB, followed by re-equilibration with MPA before the subsequent run. The elution yield under binding conditions averaged at least three BE test results.

Results and discussion
Membrane morphological, structural, and physico‑chemical properties

The reaction mechanism between the CNFs and CA (and, potentially, the CMC) involved a two-step esterification, where the carboxylic groups from both CMC and CA were first dehydrated to form different intermediates. A formation of anhydride intermediates followed when subjected to further heating, and, finally, undergoing a nucleophilic addition with dehydrated hydroxyl groups on the CNFs (and available CMC) to form ester linkages, as already well documented by previous studies (Wang et al. 2018) and presented schematically in Fig. 1.

The potentiometric titration curves (Fig. 2) of the CA, CNFs, and representative CNF-CMC- CA membranes, were performed, to confirm the crosslinking by quantification of weak acid (carboxylic, –COOH, Table 2) groups on the membranes, arising from the carboxyl content from the CMC and mono-/die-esterified CA (Kokol and Vivod 2023). The CA had three carboxylic acid groups, ionizable at pKa values of about 3.14, 4.75 and 6.40 at room temperature, while the CMC and CNFs showed one small bend at pH of around 4.0 and 4.4, respectively, given the small quantity (0.19 and 0.21 mmol/g) of

negative charge, that is related to the presence of anionic/carboxylate surface groups. These groups were obviously increased to around 1.7–3.5 mmol/g in the case of differently prepared (CMC-CNF-CA) based membranes, depending on the solid content of both CMC and CNFs, as well as the addition of CA. The only detectable pKa value for the membranes was obtained at a lower and similar pH (4–4.4) than for both CMC and CNFs, or had been shifted to a higher pH (4.5–5.4), which confirmed an increasing number of free –COOH groups, due to a high proportion of mono-esterified CA with the CNFs rather than its (bi-esterification) crosslinking, while the contribution from CMC was negligible. This effect was the most pronounced for the membrane (M3) prepared with a lower solid content of CMC than CNFs (CMC:CNF = 3.7:4.4; total 0.81 wt%), where the contribution of mono-esterified CA to the total –COOH groups was even higher, due to the shifting of its pK to higher values (pK 5–5.4), and it increased with a higher proportion of CA added, yielding in total 1.74 mmol/g (5 wt/wt% CA) and 2.0 mmol/g (10 wt/wt% CA) of –COOH groups. The membrane (M2) prepared with a higher solid content of CMC than CNFs (CMC:CNF = 4.4:2.9; total 0.74 wt%) showed a similar effect ( pK 4.4–4.6), by generating 2.45 mmol/g of carboxyls. A much slower reduction of the titration curves was shown for these samples by increasing the pH and their similar courses independent of the titration direction (forward versus backward), thus, additionally, confirming the CA mono/ bi-esterification binding to the CNFs. However, the membranes (M7) prepared with the highest solid content of CMC/CNFs (1.66 wt%) with the same weight ratio (CMC:CNF = 8.3:8.3) and 20–30 wt/wt% CA, yielded a similarly high quantity (2.2–2.5 mmol/g of –COOH groups at about a pH of 4.5, confirming the limited contribution of bi/mono-esterified CA with CNFs (its crosslinking and functionalization) to the total –COOH groups.

The swelling facilitates the disruption of the internal hydrogen bonds between the CNFs and CMC chains, which increases the accessibility of the –COOH groups on the mono-esterified CA and CMC backbone to analytes (Lys). Thus, the membranes were swelled in a mobile phase A (MPA) up to their equilibrium, frozen and lyophilized, and analyzed by SEM imaging and mercury-intrusion porosimetry. An obvious difference in surface morphology

can be seen from the SEM images of the representative membranes, presented in Fig. 3. The higher the CMC content, the more dense structure with smaller and irregularly distributed pores, can be observed,

which was additionally worsened in membranes with a higher total solid content and being prepared with a lower weight percentage of CA (i.e., 5 wt/wt%). On the other hand, an increased addition of CA (10 wt/

wt%) induced the orientation of CNFs due to their crosslinking via CA, and, consequently, directing the membrane porosity/morphology. This effect was even more pronounced in the case of membranes prepared with a higher total solid content (e.g., 1.66 wt%, M7), where the phase separations were additionally induced by the increased dry weight of CMC, resulting in longitudinal channels in a cross-section. This could influence the Lys transfer and flow rate reduction, while the type and availability of –COOH groups may affect its binding capacity (BC).

The mercury-intrusion porosimetry results of the selected membranes (M4 and M5) crosslinked with higher (10 wt/wt%) CA addition, presented in Fig. 4, followed the same trend. They showed that the membrane (M5) with higher CMC content (CMC > CNF) had higher porosity (> 86%), and higher skeletal density (~ 2.5 g/cm3), but lower total pore surface area (~ 0.76 m2/g) when compared to that prepared with higher CNF ones (CMC < CNF), which was additionally reduced/increased after HPLC analysis of the 0.5 g/L Lys solution. A half lower Hg intrusion volume was thus measured for the CMC > CNF based membrane compared to the CMC < CNF ones, and, after its HPLC analysis, due to the irreversible membrane compression during the chromatographic experiments (exposed to the pressure of 10 bars). Besides, the variable pore distribution profiles were

identified among differently prepared membranes, amongst which the CMC < CNF ones showed a pore size distribution closest to the Gaussian (Fig. S1) with the lowest average pore size (~ 85 µm) and the lowest porosity (~ 80%); both parameters increased with increasing of CNFs content (~ 94 µm, 96%) for the M5 samples with the same (1.18 wt%) total solid content. After the HPLC testing, larger pores’ domination (~ 106 µm) but lower open structures (porosity ~ 60–77%) were measured for this sample, due to too-high compressibility, consequently, resulting in CNFs assembling, as also identified by SEM imaging (Fig. 3b). The compression tests (the stress–strain curves, presented in Fig. 5a), carried out for the selected membranes (prepared with 10 wt/wt% CA), supported these results by improved mechanical properties, i.e., increased compressive stress from 3.12 kPa (M5, CMC = CNF) to 4.4 kPa (M5, CMC > CNF), 5.89 kPa (M6, CMC = CNF) and 8.08 kPa (M7, CMC = CNF) with increasing the solid content, obtained at the highest stress (ε = 70%) for the same membranes after 3-cycle testing using different deformations (ε = 30, 50 and 70%). Two obvious distinct deformation regions were also observed, a linear elastic deformation region at low strains (ε < 30%) and a densification region at large strains (ε > 40%), which shifted slightly to lower values for the membranes with higher CNF (M5) and total solid content (M7). This indicated their better compressive properties, able to bear much larger deformation. The similar profile of compressive stress–strain curves for new (previously untested) M6 and M7 membranes additionally supports this; the compression stress at maximum strain (ε = 70%) was, namely, increased to 6.21 kPa and 9.05 kPa, respectively. The membranes were able to withstand large deformation without a collapse, and almost returned to their original shape after the release of loading, as also demonstrated by the 10-cycle testing of M6 performed with or without intermediate wetting (to simulate chromatographic conditions; Fig. 5b). While the thickness of this membrane was maintained after each cycle in the case of intermediate wetting, it decreased slowly (from 4.8 mm to 3.16 mm after 7th cycle) with each subsequent cycle in the case of continuous testing without intermediate wetting—confirming its viscoelasticity. Membrane performance under static (equilibrium) conditions

The most suitable range for Lys to bind with weak anion exchanging supports is between a pH of 6–9 (Davies et al. 1969) due to the pH of positively charged Lys that is around pH 11. As revealed from the potentiometric titration analysis (Fig. 2), the pKa of membranes is at around 4.7–5, which enables electrostatic charge interactions (attraction) between the positive charge on the Lys and the negative charge on CMC/CNFs membrane chains in the window between pH 5 and 11, thus making the selection of pH 8 appropriate for our chromatographic studies.

The static (equilibrium) binding capacity (SBC) measurements revealed how the membrane microstructure and the availability/accessibility of carboxylic groups (being influenced by the presence of CMC and mono-esterified CA on CNFs) affect the equilibrium of Lys binding. It was expected that membranes with the same content of CMC versus CNFs, but using different concentrations of CA for their preparation should have different BCs as a result of different quantities of mono- versus biesterified CA, resulting in more electrostatic sites for Lys binding.
The maximum capacity of Lys adsorption was thus measured for each membrane after 24 h of

incubation in MPA containing different Lys content (0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 mg/mL) (Fig. 6a). Comparing the effect of membranes prepared with different solid content (0.88 and 1.18 wt%) and weight mass ratio of CMC:CNF and 5 wt/wt% CA, it is obvious that higher total and CMC content yielded higher Lys adsorption (e.g., from 56 to 92% for 1 mg/mL Lys) and SBC. It was also observed that the Lys adsorption (and SBC) was generally lower for the membranes prepared with 10 wt/wt% CA (yielding from 38 to 88% of Lys adsorption for 1 mg/mL Lys), compared to the same membranes prepared with lower or higher CA content, despite of bearing a quantitatively higher content of –COOH groups (Table 2). It looks like the contribution of mono-esterified CA is not fully available for Lys binding, which can also be related to the generally high porosity and low SSA of membranes (Fig. 4), reducing the possibility for interactions. A further increase of CA addition thus no longer improves the adsorption, yielding a maximum of 67%, which corresponds to the potentiometric titration results (Fig. 2, Table 2). The SBC was also increasing with increasing of Lys concentration, however, giving the membrane preparation-dependent adsorption maximums (Fig. 6b). The maximum adsorption capacity (Q) of around 682–572 mg/g was reached for the M4–M5 membranes, prepared with 10 wt/wt% CA. With a further increase of solid content (and, thus, also the CMC and mono-esterified CA; M6 and M7), the adsorptive capacity increased to around 1080 mg/g. With increasing the CA from

Membrane performance under chromatographic conditions

The chromatographic properties of an adsorption membrane are a combination of equilibrium binding capacity, adsorption kinetics, and structure, so the performance of the selected membranes was first evaluated regarding the flow rate in bind-elute (BE) tests (Fig. S2). The results showed that the pressure does not increase linearly with the flow (Fig. S2a). As the flow rate increased, either the structure of the membrane changed, or partial clogging occurred, due to the membrane pressure on the housing unit. We subsequently tried to reduce this compressibility problem of the tested membranes by increasing the total solid content (as is evident from Fig. 5), changing the weight ratio between CMC and CNFs, and increasing their crosslinking with CA. Otherwise, all the tested membranes prepared with up to the total weight of 1.18 wt% (M1–M5) or crosslinked with up to 20 wt%/wt% CA were physically stable (did not tear), and remained intact, even at very high (up to 30 bars) pressures. On the contrary, the membranes prepared with higher total solid content (> 1.66 wt%, M6–M7) and using ≥ 30 wt/wt% CA (M7) showed an obvious tendency for disintegration already at low pressure, due to the excessive cross-linking of individual segments, and, consequently, an inhomogeneous morphological structure. However, the pressure change with time of use (several hours) on the membrane was observed to be significant (few bars), reflecting on the changes of mobile phases during testing. Such behavior can be explained by the higher hydrophilicity caused by the fibrils` membrane swelling/wetting, which reduced the pore size available for the flow (that was more pronounced in the case of the more open/porous membrane, Fig. 3). At the beginning, only larger pores were wetted, while smaller pores got involved later, and could also contribute to the membrane`s chromatographic performance. At the same time, the intrinsic properties of both CMC and CNFs, above all, their highly hydrophilic and water-retention ability, due to the presence of both an abundant (still free and available) quantity of –OH groups on CNFs and –COOH groups from the CMC and mono-esterified CA on CNFs, increased the wettability of the membranes significantly, making them more compacted and also hydrophilic, thus, resulting in the reduction of MPA permeation by time.

Figure S2b presents a typical chromatogram for a BE test, where Lys binding in MPA and elution in MPB are shown. After equilibration, MPA containing a certain amount of Lys (0.5–2 mg/mL) was injected into the membrane, followed by an absorbance reading. As the membrane comes in contact with Lys under dynamic conditions, the Lys adsorbed by the membrane and its unbound quantity present in the FT fraction is evaluated, which is illustrated by the initial increase in absorbance on the chromatogram. This is not the consequence of an overloaded membrane, since the BC of Lys is between 30–65 mg/g (Fig. 7a), regardless of the membrane tested. The percentage of unbound Lys according to Eq. (4) thus varied from 5% up to 7%, due to some bypass through a membrane associated with its inhomogeneous structure. It also increases with the flow rate from 3% up to 12% when increasing the flow rate from 0.5 to 2 mL/min. After rinsing, a step change was made to elute the Lys in the MPB. The increase in ionic strength weakened the charge interactions between the Lys and membrane surface, causing the Lys to release from it, which is evidenced by the elution peak starting at about 1 min.

The elution yield under binding conditions (BE test results) for differently prepared membranes (Figs. 7a and 6b), performed at 0.5 mL/min flow rate using 0.5 mg/mL concentrated Lys solution, was thus between 78 and 99%. The Lys leakage depends primarily on the membrane microstructure (influenced by the total solid content, CMC and CNFs weight ratio and their crosslinking degree), and, secondly, on the content and availability of carboxylic groups. The leakage was thus higher (12–16%) for membranes prepared with lower total solid (M1-M5) but higher CMC content (CMC > CNF) with 5 wt/wt% CA addition, due to their higher porosity and skeletal density (Figs. 3 and 4). Comparatively, the membrane prepared with a higher CNFs content or an increased addition of CA (10 wt/wt% CA), resulted in up to 7% of Lys leakage; among them, the M4-10 membrane showed no leakage, probably due to the most morphologically appropriate membrane structure for the chromatographic application. On the other hand, the membranes prepared with even higher total solids (M6-M7) yielded the highest Lys leakage (up to 21.5%), due to their isotropic morphological structure.

The DBC tests were determined afterward using a standard frontal analysis approach (Černigoj et al. 2015; a typical measurement is presented in Fig. S2c), which yielded between 31 and 66 mg of Lys binding per g of dry M1-M4 membranes prepared with 5 wt/wt% CA, and a further increase up to 167–163 mg/g for M4-M5 membranes prepared with higher CMC content (CMC > CNF) and 10 wt/wt% CA, which corresponds well to the relative SBC values obtained for 0.5 g/L Lys adsorption after 24 h of incubation (Fig. 7a and b, where around 310–399 mg/g Lys adsorption was reached for M4–M5 membranes prepared with 10 wt/wt% CA. The DBC was increased further, up to 417 mg/g, for the M6-10CA membrane with higher solid content, while dropping to 42 mg/g for M7-10CA at similarly high (21%) leakage, although the SBC values were similar (1076–1098 mg/g for 1 mg/g Lys solution, Fig. 7c).

However, there was a clear trend of DBC decrease with increasing both the Lys concentration in MPA and the flow rate for M6-10CA membrane from 417/258 mg/g at 0.5/1 mg/mL and 0.5 mL/min down to 19/16 mg/g at 2 mL/min, which could be due to mass transfer limitations and/or compressibility issues (Fig. 5) with the increasing flow rate—being also reflected in an exponential decrease of pressure on the membrane during testing (reaching 4.5–5.1 bars at 4–3.8 mL/min followed it manometrically)— resulting in the reduction of available –COOH groups and their binding capacity (BC). This was additionally affected by multiple consecutive washing of the membranes between individual testing cycles (injection of Lys) to remove the remaining adsorbed Lys completely. The observation thus also suggests diffusion-trapped Lys within the membrane structure—above all, M7, with a longitudinally oriented channel structure (Fig. 3b) and high compressibility (Fig. 5), which was also influenced negatively by the increased flow rate. A Lys mass balance of between 84 and 95% was achieved for the tested membrane, supporting these conclusions. In comparison, the DBC for Lys of the e-spun carbon nanofibrous mats reached over 200 mg/g, and showed a high feed flow rate with a low-pressure drop (Schneiderman et al. 2011). The regenerated cellulose-based e-spun membranes reached ~ 21 mg/mL of Lys adsorption at a compressive pressure of 1 MPa (Dods et al. 2015), which was also decreasing with the pressure or the

number of bed layers due to the reduction in surface area resulting from the membrane`s compression. The DBC of existing commercial polymeric-based monoliths (CIMmultus™ SO3 Sartorius BIA Separations d.o.o.) is in the range of 50–100 mg Lys (Kodermac et al. 2025) per g of dry chromatographic support, which is lower than with the studied membranes, however, with high stability (nonsignificant pressure change) and 100% Lys recovery after repeated use; the M4 membrane is the most comparable to this (DBC ~ 68–138 mg/g, up to 1.7% leakage).

Weak cation-exchange and highly porous (> 95%) micro-structured (> 80 μm) cellulose-based membranes were prepared from carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) by variation of their weight ratio and total solid content (0.5–1.18 wt%) using a freeze-casting process, while their stability (and additional carboxylic groups from 1.7 to 2.5 mmol/g) was obtained by esterification of the available hydroxyl groups using citric acid (CA, 5 or 10 wt/wt%) mediated chemistry performed in situ during the fabrication. By increasing the total solid content and CMC, more isotropic microporous structures were formed, influencing the pressure drop and variable stability under the chromatographic mode. However, the membrane’s charge (pKa ~ 4.7–5) enabled ionic interactions with the positively charged Lys (pKa ~ 11), but its binding capacity was dependent on the membrane’s morphology and the availability of carboxylic groups on the CMC. The membranes were still able to achieve an elution yield of above 70%, a DBC for Lys between 165 and 417 mg/g, with a mass balance of 84 − 95% and > 95% recovery. The proportion of bound Lys was also reduced by increasing the flow-rate due to too high compressibility of the membranes, resulting in a more dense structure with smaller and irregularly distributed pores that limited Lys transfer and binding. By ~ 68–138 mg/g DBC and up to 1.7% leakage, the membrane prepared with a relatively middle-range of total solid content and a similar CMC:CNF weight ratio was the most comparable with the commercial chromatographic monoliths. While the prepared membranes showed promising results for batch protein adsorption (370–1080 mg/g), additional research is required
to improve their performance for a chromatographic approach.
